evidence: Quint. 1.5.50: nam et an et aut conjūnctiōnēs sunt
terms.comment: In Cicero and Quintilian the connecting word of grammar, as well as any joining. The kinds are the later grammarians’: conjūnctiōnēs cōpulātīvae, coordinating (et, atque, ac), disjūnctīvae (aut, vel), adversātīvae (sed, at), with concessīvae, temporālēs and condiciōnālēs after them (Traupman 235–236, 246). Lewis & Short gives cōpulātīvus, disjūnctīvus, adversātīvus and concessīvus from late grammarians and Martianus Capella; Priscian’s adversātīvae were what we now call concessive (quamquam, etsī). Traupman calls a subordinating conjunction conjūnctiō subjūnctīva, as Charisius does (Lewis & Short s.v. subjūnctīvus).

evidence: Quint. 1.4.18: in convīnctiōnibus autem complexūs eōrum esse jūdicāvērunt
terms.comment: Quintilian’s preferred word, as the closer rendering of Greek σύνδεσμος, though he knows that most say conjūnctiō.
